one_liner: Go userspace CSPRNG: a sync.Pool of crypto/rand-seeded ChaCha8 generators, far faster than crypto/rand for bulk and parallel reads.
what_it_does: Provides cryptographically seeded random bytes and helpers (Read, Bytes, Entropy128/192/256, Intn, Uint64n, BigIntn, Float64, Perm, Shuffle) whose methods never return errors. A master ChaCha8 generator is seeded once from crypto/rand; New() derives per-instance keys from it, and the package-level functions borrow generators from a sync.Pool. It also exposes frand.Reader (an io.Reader usable where crypto/rand.Reader is expected) and NewSource() (a math/rand v1 Source).
how_it_is_fast: Random bytes come from the ChaCha8 stream cipher keystream in userspace (Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8, partly in assembly) instead of a getrandom syscall per call, so large reads run at keystream speed. The sync.Pool gives each concurrently running goroutine its own derived generator, so there is no shared lock and throughput scales with cores. Since the 2024-10-07 commit 'switch to stdlib ChaCha8 generator', the generator itself is Go's stdlib code; frand's own contribution is the seeding, pooling and helper API (before that it was a hand-written ChaCha12 fast-key-erasure design).
when_to_use: Go services that need lots of unpredictable bytes (tokens, nonces, salts, test data) and are bottlenecked on crypto/rand.Read, especially from many goroutines at once.
Replacing math/rand in Go code where predictability is a bug: hash-table salts, randomized test cases that must differ run to run, load-balancer jitter.
Bulk fills of hundreds of KB per call, where the old README measured 5094 MB/s vs 239 MB/s for crypto/rand on 512 KB reads.
Code that wants Intn/Perm/Shuffle helpers on a secure source without handling errors on every call.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ projects: this is a pure Go module with no C ABI; for a C userspace random pool see randp or the aesctr generator in testingRNG.
Long-lived key material where you want the kernel to hold the state: the generator state lives in process memory and no new entropy is mixed in after the one-time seed (README).

Small-integer hot loops (Intn, Perm) where an insecure PRNG is acceptable: the old README table had math/rand faster (Intn 20 vs 45 ns/op, Perm(32) 789 vs 954 ns/op), and Uint64n still uses modulo with rejection rather than Lemire's nearly divisionless method (issue #3, open since 2020).
Reproducible seeded streams across versions: NewCustom output changed when the backend moved from ChaCha12 to ChaCha8, and the bufsize and rounds arguments are now ignored.
Go 1.22 and older toolchains: go.mod requires Go 1.23.1 because it depends on math/rand/v2.ChaCha8.

integration.thread_safety: Package-level functions, frand.Reader and Source (mutex-guarded) are safe for concurrent use; an *RNG from New() or NewCustom() has no internal lock, so use one per goroutine.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: frand.Reader can replace crypto/rand.Reader as an io.Reader, and NewSource() plugs into math/rand v1, but the helper functions have different signatures (no error return) and there is no math/rand/v2 Source adapter.

gotchas: Since 2024-10-07 the package is a thin wrapper over Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8; on Go 1.23+ you get most of the speed by using rand.NewChaCha8 with a crypto/rand seed yourself, and frand adds the pool and helpers.
NewCustom(seed, bufsize, rounds) silently ignores bufsize and rounds and panics unless the seed is exactly 32 bytes; the old README described the default as ChaCha12, the current code is ChaCha8.
Source.Uint64 calls Uint64n(math.MaxUint64), so it can never return 2^64-1; Source.Seed makes the stream deterministic, which removes the security property for that Source.

The README's 20x and 100x figures were measured on the pre-2024 implementation against the crypto/rand of that time; Linux's vDSO getrandom (LWN reports about 15x faster small reads than the syscall) narrows the gap on new kernels, so re-measure on your Go version and kernel.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick frand when a Go program needs a secure source that is fast and scales across goroutines; valyala/fastrand and pgregory.net/rand (sfc64) report lower per-call times in their own benchmarks but are not cryptographic, and vpxyz/xorshift is a set of plain non-crypto generators. For C/C++, randp (AES-CTR pool beating glibc arc4random) is the closest catalogued analogue.
verified_claims_summary: The current README claims 20x faster than crypto/rand for large reads and over 100x in parallel, but gives no hardware, Go version or results. The only published numbers are in the pre-2024 README for the ChaCha12 fast-key-erasure version: Read of 512 KB 5094 vs 239 MB/s (about 21x, derived from page data), and with 64 goroutines 19665 vs 191 MB/s (about 103x, derived from page data); math/rand was faster for Intn and Perm. For the ChaCha8 generator frand now wraps, a 2025 Lemire benchmark (search snippet only; code in lemire/Code-used-on-Daniel-Lemire-s-blog 2025/10/15) reports 2.6 ns vs 51 ns per uint64 for ChaCha8 vs crypto/rand on an Apple M4. That supports the order of magnitude for the generator but does not measure frand itself.
status_note: Stale since the 2024-10-07 ChaCha8 switch (22 commits, 1 open issue, 93 stars), but MIT-licensed, a single 270-line file using only the stdlib, so it is easy to vendor; usable from Go only.
